source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The value is within the expected normal range for a healthy adult and does not require confirmation or further respiratory assessment.","B":"The value is abnormally low and warrants prompt assessment, confirmation of the reading, and treatment of hypoxemia as clinically indicated.","C":"The value is above the normal range and most likely represents hyperoxemia caused by excessive oxygen delivery before the measurement was obtained.","D":"The value is clinically insignificant unless it remains below 88% for several hours, so immediate reassessment of the client is unnecessary."}}
source_row.rationale: For an adult without a known lower baseline target, an SpO2 of 88% is markedly below the usual range and warrants prompt clinical assessment, confirmation of the reading, and treatment according to the cause and the client's condition. Option B is correct. Option A incorrectly labels 88% as normal. Option C incorrectly calls the low value hyperoxemia from excessive oxygen. Option D delays reassessment despite a clinically important low reading.
source_row.source_detail: FDA — Pulse Oximeter Basics: oxygen saturation is generally 95%–100% for most healthy individuals; lower readings require interpretation with symptoms, clinical status, and known device limitations, and unexpectedly low values should be assessed/confirmed. Current FDA consumer/clinical safety information on pulse oximeters; rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Physiological Integrity — Reduction of Risk Potential: diagnostic tests, laboratory values, vital-sign monitoring and potential complications. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

source_row.stem: An adult with no known chronic hypoxemia has a pulse-oximetry reading of 88% on room air. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
